summary: Explains how the IPsec security services apply to IP multicast packets, which the base IPsec architecture mainly describes for unicast. It matters only to IPsec implementations that support multicast. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Normal secure mail goes to one person in a sealed envelope. This memo explains how to seal a message that many people receive at once, so only the right group can read it.

questions: how does ipsec work with multicast
what is a group security association
what is tunnel mode with address preservation
what is the gpad in ipsec
subtitle: How IPsec protects packets sent to a whole group, where the destination is a multicast address.

tldr.problem: The IPsec architecture mainly defines security associations between two devices, but multicast packets have a group destination address and many receivers sharing the same keys.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds optional extensions to RFC 4301: group databases (GSPD and GPAD), group security associations set up by a group key management protocol, tunnel mode with address preservation, and a re-key rollover scheme.
tldr.outcome: IPsec devices that support multicast can protect IP multicast packets and keep them routable as multicast. Devices that do not support multicast need not implement the extensions.

facts.label: Group Identifier length
facts.value: at least 4 bytes, less than 256 bytes

today: RFC 5374 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 4301 and matters only to IPsec implementations that support multicast.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 4301 describes IPsec mainly for Security Associations (SAs) shared between two devices, with a unicast destination address. It defined manually keyed transport mode SAs for multicast destinations, but not how IPsec works with a Group Key Management (GKM) protocol, nor a tunnel mode SA with a multicast address in the outer header.

This document adds OPTIONAL extensions so groups of devices can share SAs whose traffic selectors include a multicast address and whose IPsec packets keep a multicast destination. Both Any-Source Multicast (ASM) and Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) group addresses are supported, as are IPv4 broadcast and IPv6 anycast addresses. An implementation without multicast support need not implement them, and RFC 4301 semantics are unchanged unless noted.

No requirements fall on routers or other intermediate systems, and no requirements are placed on multicast routing or admission protocols. This version requires all devices in a Security Association to be homogeneous: they MUST share a common set of cryptographic transform and protocol-handling capabilities.
sections.eli5: Sending a locked box to one friend is easy. This memo explains how to lock a box so a whole club can open it, and nobody else can.

sections.title: Groups and Their Roles
sections.content:
A Group is a set of devices protecting group communications. A Group Member may be a Group Sender, a Group Receiver, or both. A Group Owner chooses the group policy. A Group Controller Key Server (GCKS) authenticates members and gives them SA policy and keying material through a Group Key Management protocol.

The two multicast service models differ in what counts as a group. In ASM, one or more senders send to one multicast address, a (*,G) group. In SSM, each sender and multicast address pair is a group, an (S,G) group.

A Group Security Association (GSA) is the collection of IPsec SAs plus the GKM SAs a member needs to receive key updates.
sections.eli5: A club has members who talk, members who listen, a boss who sets the rules, and a keeper who hands out the secret key to the right people.

sections.title: Tunnel Mode with Address Preservation
sections.content:
A host may use transport or tunnel mode for multicast, but a security gateway MUST use tunnel mode. Ordinary tunnel mode puts the gateway's own addresses in the outer header, which breaks multicast routing. Routers compare the destination address with their multicast state, and routing protocols such as PIM-SM build trees from the source and group address, so a changed source can fail Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) checks and the packet may be dropped.

In tunnel mode with address preservation the gateway copies the inner destination address into the outer header, and SHOULD also copy the inner source address. A gateway that preserves the source will not receive ICMP Path MTU messages meant for it. Address preservation applies only when the outer and inner IP versions are the same.
sections.eli5: If you put a letter in a bigger envelope, the post office must still be able to read the original address. So the outer envelope copies the same addresses.

sections.title: New and Extended Databases
sections.content:
The Group Security Policy Database (GSPD) is the SPD with multicast semantics added. Entries get an address preservation (AP) flag with AP-L for the local and AP-R for the remote tunnel address, and a directionality attribute: symmetric, sender only or receiver only. Because a multicast address must not be a source address, local and remote addresses are not swapped for entries with a remote multicast address. The outbound GSPD MUST be able to trigger a GKM registration exchange.

The SAD records whether address preservation applies. The new Group Peer Authorization Database (GPAD) links the GSPD to the GKM subsystem. It says which GCKS devices are authorized, how to authenticate each, which Group Identifiers they may serve, and which traffic selectors they may assert. The Group Identifier is a byte string of IKE ID type Key ID that MUST be at least four bytes and less than 256 bytes long. Policy that does not match an authorized data flow is discarded and the reason SHOULD be logged.
sections.eli5: The rule book gains pages for groups, and a new list of which key keepers you trust and which groups each may speak for.

sections.title: Re-Key Rollover
sections.content:
A group may hold several IPsec SAs at once: one per authorized sender if anti-replay is used, and overlapping SAs for one sender so the stream continues across a re-key. An implementation MUST support at least two concurrent IPsec SAs per Group Sender and the rollover algorithm.

The GCKS multicasts a Re-Key Event (RKE) message. The text describes two timers, counted from the start of the event. The Activation Time Delay (ATD) says how long to wait before the sender uses the new, leading edge SA, so all members can install it. The Deactivation Time Delay (DTD) says when the old, trailing edge SA is deleted, limiting exposure of retired keys. Group policy may choose other timer values.
sections.eli5: When the club changes its secret key, everyone first gets the new key, and only then does the speaker use it. The old key is thrown away a little later.

sections.title: Data Origin Authentication
sections.content:
A MAC with one shared secret cannot show who sent a packet in a group of more than two, because every member can create a valid tag. When origin authentication is needed, an algorithm such as TESLA (RFC 4082) or an RSA digital signature (RFC 4359) should be used.

Signatures cost much more than an HMAC, so to resist denial-of-service from non-members the signed SA may be wrapped in an SA using a MAC. This needs a second pass across the IPsec boundary, because AH and ESP define an ICV for only one authenticator transform.
sections.eli5: If everyone shares one stamp, anyone can fake a note from anyone else. A personal signature proves who wrote it, but it takes longer to check.

sections.title: Packet Processing
sections.content:
Processing follows Section 5 of RFC 4301 with amendments. Outbound, if address preservation is marked in the SAD entry, the outer source and/or destination address is copied from the inner header, and it MUST NOT be marked when IP versions differ.

Inbound, a device must accept IPsec packets not addressed to itself, because the outer destination may be a multicast group. An added step 3aa looks up multicast AH or ESP packets in the SAD by SPI and destination (and source if applicable); if there is no match the packet goes to SPD-I lookup. A new item 6 requires that preserved outer addresses match the inner ones. If they do not, the system MUST discard the packet and treat it as an auditable event.
sections.eli5: On arrival, the receiver opens the outer envelope and checks that the address on it matches the one on the inner letter. If not, it throws the letter away and notes it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions provide group confidentiality and integrity with shared keys, sender authentication through signatures or TESLA, limited anti-replay using sequence numbers, and filtering of traffic from unauthorized senders by DISCARD policy.

They do not stop outside attackers who flood the group, compromise a multicast router, or replay old packets to a group without anti-replay. For large any-source groups, anti-replay state per sender is impractical. Insiders are also a risk: security is no stronger than the weakest admitted member, who could leak keys or forge packets.

Deployment issues include groups with mixed cryptographic capability, groups spanning policy domains, and SSM senders whose source address changes. For SSM, the RFC recommends a default DISCARD policy for unauthorized sender addresses.
sections.eli5: A shared key keeps outsiders out, but if one club member leaks the key or cheats, the lock cannot help. Picking trustworthy members matters most.

viz.caption: ROLES IN A SECURE MULTICAST GROUP

items.title: Group Owner
items.text: Chooses the policy for the group.

items.title: GCKS
items.text: Authenticates members and provides SA policy and keys.

items.title: Group Sender
items.text: A member authorized to send to the group.

items.title: Group Receiver
items.text: A member authorized to receive what senders send.
